titre: He asked for the DNA test that would set him free
accroche: Maryland, 1993: a man on death row gets, by sheer persistence, the genetic test no one wanted to grant him. It clears him.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1984, in Maryland, a nine-year-old girl, Dawn Hamilton, is found raped and murdered. An anonymous tip and eyewitness accounts place Kirk Bloodsworth, a former Marine working in the area as a waterman, near the scene shortly before the crime. In 1985, he is convicted and sent to death row, with no physical evidence tying him to the crime. His death sentence is later commuted to two consecutive life sentences.

## A prisoner reads a story

In 1992, still in prison, Bloodsworth reads an account of an English case in which genetic analysis cleared one suspect before pointing to another. He realizes that a similar technique might exist for his own case: a biological sample left on the victim had been preserved. With the help of his lawyer, he demands that it be compared with his own profile.

## What the test shows

The result, obtained in 1993, formally excludes Bloodsworth: the semen found on the victim does not match his DNA. He is released in June 1993, after more than nine years behind bars, part of them on death row. It is the first case in the United States of a death row inmate exonerated by post-conviction DNA testing.

## A name found ten years later

The identity of the real perpetrator remains unknown for another decade. In 2003, Maryland runs the preserved genetic profile against its database of convicted offenders and gets a match: Kimberly Shay Ruffner, an inmate Bloodsworth had rubbed shoulders with in prison without knowing he was guilty, sentenced to 45 years one month after the murder for a separate burglary and assault. Ruffner pleads guilty to the murder of Dawn Hamilton in 2004.

## The shift

Bloodsworth's story does not pit science against judicial error: it shows DNA repairing what eyewitness testimony, given in good faith but fallible, had produced. It also has an institutional sequel: the 2004 federal Innocence Protection Act creates a grant program that bears his name, to fund post-conviction DNA testing in states that lack it. One man had to read the account of a similar case and press for the examination that would get him out: what was missing for the longest time was not the technique, but access to it.

repere.texte: In June 1993, Kirk Bloodsworth becomes the first death row inmate in the United States exonerated by post-conviction DNA testing, after more than nine years behind bars.
repere.source: National Library of Medicine (National Institutes of Health), “Visible Proofs,” Kirk Bloodsworth case file

carte.punch: He read the story of a similar case and walked off death row
carte.idee: Sentenced to death in 1985 for a murder he did not commit, Kirk Bloodsworth learns in prison that DNA tests exist and gets the sample from his case compared with his own. In June 1993, the result excludes him and sets him free.
carte.source_courte: National Library of Medicine (NIH), United States

quiz.question: How does Kirk Bloodsworth obtain, in 1993, the test that clears him?
choix: A federal judge orders a new DNA test on his own initiative after the case is reopened
The police find a new suspect and themselves request the DNA comparison
He reads the account of a comparable case and demands that a preserved sample be compared
His lawyer discovers a procedural error that automatically voids his conviction
quiz.explication: It is Bloodsworth himself who, in 1992, learns from reading an account that this type of test exists and insists that the biological sample preserved in his file be compared with his genetic profile. The result, in 1993, formally excludes him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is identified as the author of Dawn Hamilton's murder, and when?
choix: A police officer who took part in the original investigation, identified in 1995 through his own confession
Kimberly Shay Ruffner, identified in 2003 through a match in the DNA database
One of the trial's eyewitnesses, exposed in 1998 by a new fingerprint analysis
A suspect never found, the case officially remaining unsolved to this day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2003, Maryland runs the preserved genetic profile against its database of convicted offenders and gets a match with Kimberly Shay Ruffner, an inmate Bloodsworth had rubbed shoulders with in prison. Ruffner pleads guilty to the murder in 2004.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What institution is created in connection with the Bloodsworth case, according to the entry?
choix: A federal laboratory tasked with centralizing all biological samples from death row inmates
A federal grant program, created in 2004, to fund post-conviction DNA testing
A standing commission tasked with automatically reviewing all death sentences handed down
A national registry of judicial errors that any convict who asks can freely consult
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2004 federal Innocence Protection Act creates a grant program bearing Kirk Bloodsworth's name, meant to help states fund post-conviction DNA testing for other cases like his.
